newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgaria president brings no quick economic fix.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgaria president brings no quick economic fix.

text.p: New Bulgarian president Petar Stoyanov formally took office on Wednesday with little sign of an economic revival as politicians remained far apart on solutions to the country's deepening crisis.

"Too many things in the Bulgarian economy are beyond control," economist Roumen Avramov of the independent think tank, the Institute for Liberal Strategies told Reuters. "The best solution for the economic problems lies...(in) immediate general elections."

Bulgaria, which has no government at the moment, is weighed down under a domestic debt exceeding a trillion levs ($1.4 billion), a total of $1.3 billion foreign debt payments due this year alone and pending grain and fuel shortages.
Its only solution is in radical reform programmes funded by multilaterals, analysts said.
As Stoyanov took office in a modest, yet colourful ceremony, the lev reached a new all-time low and local media published forecasts of uncontrollable hyperinflation.

"Bulgaria will not escape hyperinflation...the bitter cup must be drunk to the bottom," former finance minister and current head of Central Cooperative Bank, Stoyan Alexandrov said in an interview with the Trud daily.

Hyperinflation will melt down the domestic debt along with people's savings, but a new government could bring in a fixed exchange rate regime run by a currency board which would stablise the crumbling financial system.
Both the opposition and ruling ex-communists see the implementation of a strict monetary regime as the solution to the country's grave economic crisis but disagree on tactics.
As daily street rallies reached their 16th day on Wednesday the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) remained adamant on their demand for early elections.
The opposition says that if early elections were held in March, the new parliament would adopt the legal amendments needed to introduce a currency board in May.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) proposed the introduction of a currency board in November as a last resort to haul the country from the brink of debt default and stabilise the collapsing national currency.
The lev traded around 800 to the dollar on Wednesday, compared to 70 a year ago.

The Fund had begun talks with the outgoing Socialist government, which resigned on December 21, on the implementation of the currency board system which severely curbs financial powers of the government and the central bank.
Talks were expected to be completed after parliament approved a new Socialist government by mid-January.
The Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), composed largely of ex-communists, has offered elections by the end of the year and a second Socialist cabinet in the meantime.
"The agony will be prolonged if instead of elections a second Socialist government is formed," said Avramov.
"It will be legitimate but will lack both domestic and foreign support, which will inevitably lead to a new political crisis and elections," he added.
The Socialist prime minister-designate Nikolai Dobrev presented a short-term programme for his planned government to the Socialist leadership on Sunday.

It included economic stabilisation measures based on IMF recommendations like implementing a currency board mechanism, stabilising collapsing banks, improving tax revenue and closing loss-making state firms.
"Holding elections now would be suicidal," Dobrev told journalists recently, adding that the BSP is the only political force with a ready anti-crisis package.
However, economists said that the plan was the opposite of what the Socialists have been doing in the past two years, since they came to power in 1994. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
